us19_service.topic: Conscription vs volunteer force; Haredi exemption and the 2024 ruling; reservists; veterans' care

claims.text: High Court of Justice, 25 June 2024, nine justices unanimous (ruling by acting president Uzi Vogelman): no legal framework distinguishes yeshiva students from others liable under the Defense Service Law; the government's exemption decision 'instructed the military authorities to apply illegitimate selective enforcement'; state funding to yeshivas and kollels for students without lawful exemption or deferral must end; about 400 yeshiva students exempted in 1949, about 63,000 by end of June 2023 (state figures); petitioners included the Movement for Quality Government, Brothers in Arms and 240 mothers of combat soldiers

IDF to Knesset FADC (Times of Israel, 20 Jan 2026): about 30,000 designated draft evaders, half Haredi; about 80,000 Haredi men aged 18-24 eligible but not enlisted; 'tens of thousands' of orders since 2024; over 530 enlisted in one week; arrests of yeshiva students; IDF needs 12,000 recruits; Bismuth bill would restore blanket exemptions and half of lost funding; chief of staff Zamir asked to return men's service to 36 months

Security Service Law (Amendment No. 28 - Temporary Order), cancelling arrests of Haredi draft evaders, passed 14 July 2026 by 58-54; on 15 July Justice Ofer Grosskopf issued an interim order suspending it pending an expanded-panel hearing

Jerusalem Post, 2 Aug 2026: High Court has frozen the arrests law and not yet ruled; Yisrael Beytenu petitioned; Katz voted for it; Zamir warned it would create national security problems; Netanyahu reportedly (KAN, N12, unconfirmed) said he would not advance it after the election and would seek a full conscription law

Defense Service Law 1949: 30 months men, 18 women; 1968 temporary order 36/24; men 32 months since 2015; reserve duty eligibility to age 40; Druze and Circassian men conscripted (Druze since 1956), non-Druze Arab citizens not conscripted but may volunteer; religious Jewish women exempt; 2013: 26% of potential conscripts exempted, 13.5% for religious reasons; 2019: 69% of Jewish men and 59% of Jewish women drafted
US moved to an all-volunteer force in 1973 after the Gates Commission; Army missed its 2022 recruiting goal by 15,000

US active-duty end strength never below 2.0 million in the Cold War, peak over 3.5 million (Korea, Vietnam); 2.1 million in 1989, falling to 1.4 million by 1999; FY2005 authorised ~1.41 million (sum of services)
Active-duty end strength enacted FY2024 1,284,500; FY2025 1,276,700 (Army 442,300, Navy 332,300, Marines 172,300, Air Force 320,000, Space Force 9,800)
Pew: veterans were about 18% of US adults in 1980 and 6% in 2022; 18.3 million veterans; active duty fell from 3.5 million in 1968 to about 1.3 million, under 1% of adults
FY2026 NDAA mandated automatic Selective Service registration of men 18-25, to begin as early as December 2026; no draft has been activated since 1973

Taub Center (July 2026): average reservist served 233 cumulative days since 7 Oct 2023; about 110,000 reservists are parents; conservative long-term wage loss at least ~4.7%, 5.8-6.4% for fathers with 290-320 days (100,000+), ~19-21% on the literature average; 30% of salaried female spouses saw wage cuts, 3% dismissed; ~70,000 students served in 2024/25; NII pays reservist benefits

Ynet 27 July 2025: 18,500 soldiers treated by the Defense Ministry Rehabilitation Department since 7 Oct 2023; 3,769 recognised with PTSD; over 10,000 in mental-health treatment; ministry projects about 100,000 wounded and disabled veterans by 2028
JNS 8 Dec 2025: more than 82,000 people treated by Israel's Defense Ministry rehabilitation system, 22,000 of them since 7 Oct 2023

CRS R48968: VA FY2026 enacted $445.49bn (mandatory $312.30bn, discretionary $133.18bn), up 21.15% from $367.71bn in FY2025; ~17.6m veterans, ~9.2m enrolled in VA health care, ~6.8m unique veteran patients; compensation to 6,456,252 veterans; disability compensation recipients 3.3m (2011) to 5.8m (2024); VA appropriations $37.47bn (FY1995) to $326.38bn (FY2025), $72.20bn to $391.03bn in 2025 dollars; PACT Act Toxic Exposures Fund $108.90bn FY2022-26

us19_spending.topic: Defence spending over time; who pays for Iron Dome and missile defence

claims.text: OMB data via CRS: US national defense outlays as % of GDP: 9.4% (FY1968), 5.5% (1975), 4.9% (1980), 6.1% (1985), 6.2% (1986), 5.2% (1990), 3.7% (1995), 3.0% (2000), 2.9% (2001); defense discretionary outlays as share of total federal outlays 22.8% (1980), 27.6% (1986), 23.9% (1990), 16.3% (2000)

SIPRI 2025: US $954bn, -7.5% real from 2024, 11% above 2016, 3.1% of GDP (3.4% in 2016), 33% of world spending; Israel $48.3bn, -4.9% real, 120% above 2016, 7.8% of GDP (5.2% in 2016), 1.7% of world; world $2,887bn

CRS: MOU missile defence $500m a year (FY2019-28), split roughly $300m RDT&E and $200m procurement/coproduction; Israel matches US RDT&E contributions; at least 50% of procurement funds spent in the US; missile-defence obligations $7,411m 1946-2020, $500m 2021, $1,500m 2022, $500m 2023, $5,700m 2024, $500m 2025, total $16,111m

CRS Table 5, US appropriations FY2006-FY2025 cumulative: Iron Dome $6,075m (first funds $205m FY2011; FY2022 $1,108m incl. $1bn supplemental), David's Sling $3,828m, Arrow II $2,145m, Arrow III $1,568m, Iron Beam $1,200m, all $14,817m; Arrow programme FY1990-2025 $4,755m; US funds just under half of annual Arrow development; Israel developed Iron Dome alone and kept proprietary rights; US co-production workshare 30% (2023 testimony)
CRS: P.L. 118-50 (April 2024) $4bn missile defence and $1.2bn Iron Beam; two US Army Iron Dome batteries transferred, announced 24 Oct 2023, described as leased under an FMS case
